scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Ten newly authored B2 assessment items requiring interpretation, argument analysis and transfer. Teacher content approval pending; no learner-facing publication.

tabs.title: Meaning and Implications
tabs.description: Interpret the message and its assumptions.

tabs.title: Reasoning and Structure
tabs.description: Evaluate how the writer supports and qualifies claims.

tabs.title: Applying the Ideas
tabs.description: Apply the author's reasoning to new realistic situations.

questions.q: Why might a well-meant suggestion be difficult for a student who usually earns high marks?
choices: The suggestion may ignore what the student has achieved in the past.
The student may hear a criticism of the work as a verdict on their ability.
High grades may leave the student with few opportunities to ask questions.
The teacher's advice may focus too heavily on the student's feelings.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that criticism of a particular performance can be mistaken for a judgement about the student's intelligence.

questions.q: What could the student achieve by taking one rewritten paragraph to the meeting?
choices: Provide grounds for replacing the original mark with a higher one.
Show that the teacher's criticism is no longer relevant to the argument.
Demonstrate that the original essay was well structured after all.
Turn a general comment into a concrete revision that can be discussed.
questions.explanation: The student tests a better way of organising evidence while keeping the original grade unchanged.

questions.q: What wider problem does the writer imply can arise when marking rewards a narrow style of writing?
choices: Students may avoid discussing the quality of their argument in favour of their grades.
A teacher may find it difficult to compare essays that use different vocabulary.
A defensible argument may be undervalued because of how it is presented.
Feedback may become more detailed without becoming easier to understand.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three observes that a grading system can favour one style, which may not adequately reflect the quality of every argument.

questions.q: Why are the two possible reactions to the essay grade presented side by side?
choices: To show that the mark may stay unchanged while the opportunity to learn differs.
To suggest that disappointment must disappear before a student can revise.
To explain why the teacher should reassess the original marking criteria.
To demonstrate that a full rewrite is necessary before any useful meeting.
questions.explanation: Both choices leave the original mark unchanged; examining the feedback can nevertheless improve future work.

questions.q: Which description best captures the writer's attitude towards students who feel hurt by criticism?
choices: Impatient: students are responsible for controlling every emotional reaction.
Detached: feelings have little connection with the way feedback is understood.
Sceptical: students who take criticism personally rarely benefit from advice.
Sympathetic: the reaction is understandable, but it need not end reflection.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one calls the reaction understandable, while paragraph four argues that disappointment should not end the conversation.

questions.q: What is the main reason for extending the discussion to coaches, colleagues and friends?
choices: To compare the reliability of professional advice with that of teachers.
To show that weighing comments against evidence matters outside school too.
To identify better sources of advice for people disappointed by their grades.
To suggest that informal feedback is less upsetting than written comments.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph applies the need to evaluate criticism to non-school contexts without treating the adviser as infallible.

questions.q: A student believes the teacher has missed a link between two claims in an essay. What is the best next step?
choices: Ask whether noticing the link would have changed the original grade.
Rewrite the entire essay in the teacher's style before discussing the link.
Show the relevant passages and ask where the reasoning remains unclear.
Retain the paragraph unchanged because the intended connection is obvious.
questions.explanation: The writer recommends specific questions and examination of evidence rather than either automatic rejection or blind acceptance.

questions.q: A classmate says, 'If criticism makes you upset, it cannot help you learn.' Which reply reflects the article most accurately?
choices: Strong emotions are a sign that the teacher's point is probably correct.
Criticism should be useful only when it is expressed without disappointment.
A learner needs to stop feeling disappointed before considering any advice.
Feeling uncomfortable does not determine whether advice is worth examining.
questions.explanation: The conclusion distinguishes the discomfort criticism can cause from its potential value when examined critically.

questions.q: A student revises an essay solely to have the original mark increased. What useful outcome might this goal overlook?
choices: Discovering which types of comments the teacher is willing to withdraw.
Developing a clearer way to connect claims and evidence in later essays.
Learning the exact wording preferred in the school's marking scheme.
Finding out whether the teacher would accept a different essay topic.
questions.explanation: The essay example treats the revised paragraph as preparation for stronger future work, not as a way to change the old mark.

questions.q: A coach comments on an athlete's performance after seeing only one training session. What response fits the writer's reasoning?
choices: Compare the observation with further evidence and test a focused change.
Follow the advice first and ask whether it was accurate afterwards.
Wait for a second expert before taking any practical step at all.
Treat the observation as too limited to provide useful information.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph recognises that a partial observation may identify a genuine weakness while still requiring evaluation.
